cover.headline: India's explosives leader turned defence exporter: the growth is real, but the price already pays for it, and Omnia adds debt rather than value
cover.lead: Solar makes a quarter of India's commercial explosives, runs plants in 11 countries and has built, in a decade, a defence business that sold ₹2,634 cr in FY26 (from ₹249 cr in FY22): explosives for missiles, propellants, Pinaka rockets, ammunition and drones. Q1FY27 was excellent: revenue +70%, profit +89%, with defence +123%. Management targets ₹14,000 cr of revenue in FY27 (+42%) and ₹4,500 cr from defence. On 14-Sep-2026 it agreed to buy South Africa's Omnia for ₹12,951 cr in cash, which would double revenue at half the margin. The street values Solar on **P/E (50-70x FY28-Sep-28E EPS)**. We forecast organic EPS of ₹267 / ₹320 / ₹379 for FY27-29E, close to the street for FY27 and ~5-7% below PL for FY28-29. Applying **50x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹350** gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with SELL.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹15,830, DCF ₹6,241. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Defence revenue grew ~80% a year over FY22-26 to 27% of sales; the defence order book is ~₹18,000 cr (Pinaka ~₹6,000 cr, exports ~₹11,000 cr). The defence subsidiary earned a 30% pre-tax margin in FY26, which is why group EBITDA margin rose from 19% (FY23) to 28%. We model defence at ₹{{as.businessLines.FY27E.defence|num}} / {{as.businessLines.FY28E.defence|num}} / {{as.businessLines.FY29E.defence|num}} cr.

arguments.h: But it is mostly exports, and the book has stopped growing
arguments.p: 60% of FY26 revenue was billed outside India; after international explosives that leaves ~₹2,000 cr, which we infer is mainly defence exports, ~75% of defence. The defence order book was ~₹18,000 cr in both Mar-26 and Jun-26: execution now runs ahead of new orders. Exports are lumpy and policy-exposed.

arguments.h: Explosives: steady volumes, inflated by price in FY27
arguments.p: Domestic explosives grew only 3% in FY26 as coal overburden removal fell; FY27's guided +30-33% for explosives is 18-20% price as ammonium nitrate costs are passed on. International grew 32% in FY26 and should grow ~30% in FY27 (Omnia excluded). Price pass-through lifts revenue, not profit: we hold EBITDA margin at {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}}-{{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}}.

arguments.h: Valuation: above its own history; Omnia does not change the math
arguments.p: At ₹19,700 Solar trades at 61.6x our FY28E EPS vs a 46.5x median forward P/E since 2021. Our 50x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}. Omnia, on a full year, would add ~₹420 cr of pre-tax profit (~10% of ours) for ~₹11,900 cr of net debt; at 6-10x EBITDA it is worth −₹170 to +₹590 a share to Solar.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): defence run-rate against the ₹4,500 cr target, working-capital release, margins as ammonium nitrate costs pass through.
Omnia: shareholder vote, competition and regulatory approvals and the final funding structure; completion expected early-to-mid 2027.
Defence orders: Pinaka follow-ons (Mk2, guided, replenishment), Bhargavastra counter-drone trials (management: complete in calendar 2026), 155 mm qualification, further export orders.
Ammonium nitrate prices and coal overburden removal after a weak FY26; the new Dhule, Odisha and South India plants.
Capex delivery (₹2,050 cr in FY27) and whether new capacity earns its cost while debt rises.

sections.title: Explosives for mines, and now rockets, shells and drones for armies

blocks.p: Solar Industries makes the explosives that break rock in coal, iron-ore and limestone mines, quarries and tunnels, and the detonators and cords that set them off ("initiating systems"). It sells **bulk explosives** (emulsions pumped into blast holes at the mine, often from trucks), **packaged explosives** (cartridges; management calls Solar the world's largest maker) and **initiating systems**. Since about 2010 it has added **defence**: high-energy materials (HMX, RDX, TNT), propellants for the Akash, Pinaka and BrahMos missiles, complete Pinaka rockets, warheads, 23-155 mm ammunition, Nagastra loitering munitions (drones that dive onto a target) and the Bhargavastra counter-drone system now in trials. The company reports one segment; its fact sheets split revenue by customer.

sections.title: Two industries: a slow-growing, price-led explosives market and a fast-growing defence market

blocks.p: India produced about 2.3 million tonnes of commercial explosives in FY25, up from 1.5 million in FY20 (~9% a year, PESO data via MOFSL). Mining, mostly coal, takes a substantial share (AR FY26); the rest goes to quarries, roads, tunnels and dams. Demand follows overburden removal (the rock stripped to reach coal) more than coal output itself. FY26 was weak: coal output was "quite muted" at 1,036 mt as heavy rain cut Coal India and Singareni production, though captive and commercial mines grew 10%. Explosives are sold largely by tender, so suppliers compete on cost, and ammonium nitrate (the main input) is passed on with a lag.

Defence is a different market. India's defence capital spending is expected to grow ~16% a year for four years and private companies' share of listed defence revenue rose from 9% to 16% over FY23-26 (Jefferies). Abroad, wars in Europe and West Asia have created a shortage of artillery shells, rockets and explosives, with demand visibility of 5-7 years (AR FY26). Solar sits at the intersection: it makes the energetic materials every munition needs and is integrating up into complete rockets and drones.

Key raw-material prices rose 30-40% (ICICI Direct, Aug-2026); Solar raised prices, and contracts carry rise-and-fall clauses, but pass-through covers ~60% of an increase (MD). In FY22-23 a similar spike lifted revenue 57% and 75% while EBITDA margin fell to ~19%.

Jefferies (Sep-2026): India's domestic defence capex to grow ~16% a year for four years; private firms' share of listed defence revenue rose from 9% (FY23) to 16% (FY26); defence exports to grow ~11% a year to ₹58,400 cr by FY30.

AR FY26: 'well-documented global shortage of medium and large calibre ammunition, especially 155mm'; demand visibility of 5-7 years as Europe, Asia and the Middle East restock. Solar's defence order book includes ~₹11,000 cr of international orders (MOFSL).
Traditional electric detonators banned from Jul-2025, moving the industry to electronic systems; the Explosives Regulation Bill 2025 replaces century-old law with digital licensing and tracking.
Orica, Dyno Nobel, Enaex, EPC earn ~14-20% EBITDA margins and trade at ~6-8x EV/EBITDA (PL, Bloomberg). Solar agreed to buy Omnia (BME) in Sep-2026 for ~8x.

Kalyani group reported to be entering explosives (Nomura question, May-2026); Munitions India (state-owned) shares the Pinaka order; Premier Explosives and others in propellants. Domestic mining tenders are price-led (Coal India buys on tender).

bullets: **What it is.** Bulk and packaged explosives and detonators for Indian mines and construction: ₹3,343 cr in FY26 (34% of revenue), ~21% a year since FY21. Coal India alone bought ₹924 cr; Solar supplies ~20-23% of CIL's explosives.

**Price, not volume, drives the big years.** FY23 realisation jumped 39% as ammonium nitrate spiked; FY24 it fell 32% and revenue with it. Volumes grew ~7-22% a year in FY22-25, faster than the market, so share rose to ~26%.

**FY26 was flat** (+3%): heavy monsoons cut CIL and Singareni output and overburden removal "was on a negative side" (MD). **Q1FY27 rebounded +52%**, helped by new plants near customers (Dhule, North India) and AN price pass-through (management: 18-20% of FY27 explosives growth is price).
**Competition:** a price-led tender market with established rivals and a possible new entrant (Kalyani group); management: "we cannot say that we will have 100% market share".

blocks.callout: **Our view:** a solid, cash-generating base with real scale advantages, but not where the growth or the premium comes from. We model ₹{{as.businessLines.FY27E.domestic|num}} cr in FY27E (+30%, mostly price), then +10% and +11% as prices normalise and volumes grow high single digits.

sections.title: International: a decade of plant-building in Africa and Turkey is now paying off

pair.title: International revenue by quarter
Five times FY20 in six years

bullets: **What it is.** Explosives exported from India plus output of plants in Zambia, South Africa (Middelburg, Problast services), Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Turkey, Kazakhstan, Thailand and Indonesia: ₹3,815 cr in FY26 (+32%), 39% of revenue. Africa brings ~US$300 mn a year (MD, Sep-2026).
**Why it took off.** Exports and overseas stalled at ~₹800 cr in 2018-21 while plants were built and customers qualified them; revenue reached ~₹1,400 cr in FY22 and ₹3,815 cr in FY26 (MD).
**Growth outlook.** Management: world mining-explosives demand grows 2-3% a year, Solar ~10% in volume and ~15% in value; FY27 ~+30% (price helps). Q1FY27 +65%.

**Profitability is uneven.** South Africa earned ₹83 cr on ₹1,083 cr of turnover, Ghana ₹83 cr on ₹413 cr, but Turkey (₹994 cr turnover) was at a small loss and its hyperinflation accounting cost ₹94.5 cr in FY26 (₹65 cr in FY25). Subsidiaries' margins were "subdued" in H1FY26 and improved from Q3 (MD).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** a genuine growth engine where Solar is gaining share against much larger global players (Orica, Dyno Nobel, Enaex). We model ₹{{as.businessLines.FY27E.intl|num}} / {{as.businessLines.FY28E.intl|num}} / {{as.businessLines.FY29E.intl|num}} cr for FY27-29E, organic only. Omnia would add ~₹13,000-15,000 cr a year, mostly in Africa, at about half Solar's margin.

Order book covers ~4 years of FY27 defence revenue

bullets: **What it is.** Energetic materials (HMX, RDX, TNT and their compounds), composite propellants for Akash, Pinaka and BrahMos, complete Pinaka rockets, warheads, mines, bombs, 30/81/155 mm ammunition, multi-mode hand grenades, Nagastra loitering munitions, MALE-class UAV and counter-drone programmes. Most sits in Solar Defence and Aerospace, which earned ₹474 cr pre-tax on ₹1,577 cr of turnover in FY26.

**Orders.** Defence order book ~₹18,000 cr at Mar-26 and Jun-26: ~₹6,000 cr Pinaka (Feb-2025 MoD contract) and ~₹11,000 cr international (MOFSL); export wins include ₹1,076 cr (29-May-2026) and ₹830 cr and ₹589 cr (Jan-2026), each over three to four years.

**Exports dominate.** Revenue billed outside India was ₹5,790 cr in FY26 vs ₹3,815 cr of international explosives; the ~₹2,000 cr difference is, we think, mainly defence exports (~75% of defence revenue). Solar does not disclose the split.

**Pipeline.** Pinaka follow-ons (guided, Mk2, replenishment, Armenia exports), Bhargavastra trials "in this calendar year", 155 mm complete rounds after a coupling facility, medium-calibre ammunition in qualification; Project Kusha and MALE UAVs are longer-dated (PL, MOFSL).

**What can go wrong.** Trials take "longer time than what we expect" (MD); export orders depend on governments, conflicts and Indian export licences; the defence order book was flat between Mar-26 and Jun-26 after revenue doubled in FY26.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is the best business in the group and the reason the stock trades at 60x. We model ₹{{as.businessLines.FY27E.defence|num}} cr in FY27E (guidance), then +31% and +25%, which the existing book can cover; PL and MOFSL are 3-5% higher for FY28. Defence reaches 38% of revenue in FY29E. Upside needs new platform orders; downside is execution slippage on lumpy export contracts.

sections.title: Omnia: a large, cheap, low-margin business bought with debt; roughly value-neutral at the price paid

blocks.p: On 14-Sep-2026 Solar agreed to buy 100% of Johannesburg-listed Omnia Holdings for ZAR 134.5 a share in cash: about US$1.355 bn or ₹12,951 cr, Solar's largest deal by far. Founded 1953, Johannesburg; 23 countries, 70+ distribution centres, 3,500+ employees. FY26 (Mar) revenue ZAR 24.2 bn (~US$1.41 bn, ₹13,307 cr): agriculture 54%, mining (BME: bulk and packaged explosives, AXXIS electronic detonators, blasting services) 41%, chemicals (Protea) 5%. Segment EBITDA ZAR 2.98 bn (agri 1.66, mining 1.31, chemicals 0.01); net cash ~US$110 mn. Owns nitric acid / ammonium nitrate plants (largest in the region). Completion needs Omnia shareholders, competition and other regulators, and is expected in early-to-mid 2027. Solar's stock fell ~17% in two days. We keep Omnia **out of our forecasts and target** until it closes and the funding is fixed, as PL and Goldman Sachs do (MOFSL includes it), and show its effect here.

bullets: **Street pro formas differ widely.** PL: EPS +2% in FY28E (half-year consolidation) and +9% in FY29E, with EBITDA margin falling from ~27.5% to ~19-20%, and Omnia worth ~₹754 a share at 12x/10x EV/EBITDA. Goldman Sachs: +11-25% to FY28 EPS. Kotak: accretion depends on synergies and funding.

**The strategic case is real.** Omnia owns the region's largest ammonium nitrate and nitric acid plants (Solar's key input), the BME mining brand with AXXIS electronic detonators, and a footprint in 23 countries including Canada, Australia and Indonesia; manufacturing would rise from 11 to ~25 countries.

**The costs are also real.** 54% of Omnia's revenue is agriculture (fertilisers, biostimulants), a business Solar does not know; chemicals is being restructured; group margins halve; Solar's debt rises about seven-fold; and integration spans two continents.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** at ~8x EBITDA Solar is not overpaying for a business that trades at 4-8x, but it is buying lower-quality earnings with debt. Value per share is close to zero at the price paid (± a few hundred rupees, ~1-3% of the share price) unless synergies come through. The bigger effect may be on the multiple: half of revenue would come from a ~13%-margin mining and agri business, and the market should not pay defence multiples for that.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: a cost moat in explosives, a capability lead in defence, no pricing power

verdicts: ~26% of India's explosives volume (FY25), the world's largest packaged-explosives maker (MD); plants near mines; emulsifiers, detonator shells, PETN, TNT and RDX made in-house.
Lowest-cost supplier in a tender market.
Explosives need PESO licences; defence products need years of trials; Solar was first private firm to dispatch Pinaka Enhanced Mk-I rockets.
Slows new entrants, does not stop funded ones (Kalyani).
Coal India (10% of revenue) buys by tender; pass-through of input costs covers ~60% of an increase.
Margins in explosives are earned on cost, not price.
No captive ammonium nitrate; FY22-23 spike cut margins to ~19%. Omnia's AN plant would change this in southern Africa only.
Integrated from explosives to rockets and drones; defence revenue ₹2,634 cr (FY26) from ₹249 cr (FY22); SDAL 30% pre-tax margin.
The source of the premium, and of the risk.
Plants in 11 countries; international revenue ₹3,815 cr; but rivals are Orica, Dyno Nobel, Enaex, AEL; Turkey subsidiary ~break-even.
Real growth engine, not a moat.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (company filings, calls and broker notes to Sep-2026)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Solar has a real but narrow moat. In explosives it is the scale, low-cost, licensed incumbent close to the mines, which wins tenders and share, but tender buyers set the price and ammonium nitrate is bought in. In defence it has a genuine capability lead among Indian private firms (integrated from energetic materials to complete rockets), which is why defence margins are higher; but that lead is being contested by well-funded groups, it depends on government trials and export licences, and it is young. The premium the market pays assumes the defence lead converts into a decade of large orders. That is possible, not proven.

sections.title: Ten years of 21% growth, with one input-cost boom and bust and a defence-led margin step-up

blocks.p: Solar's revenue grew from ₹1,449 cr in FY16 to ₹9,838 cr in FY26, about 21% a year, and net profit from ₹178 cr to ₹1,737 cr, about 26% a year. The path had three phases. Until FY21 it was a pure explosives company (exports and overseas already ~35-42% of sales) growing ~12% a year with a ~20% EBITDA margin. In FY22-23 the ammonium nitrate (AN) price spike after the Russia-Ukraine war pushed revenue up 57% and 75% (prices are passed on), while the margin slipped to ~19%; when AN fell, FY24 revenue dropped 12%. Since FY24 defence has changed the mix: defence rose from 9% of revenue in FY24 to 27% in FY26, and EBITDA margin rose from 19% in FY23 to 28% in FY26.

pair.title: Revenue: 21% a year, with an AN-price bulge in FY23
Net profit: up six times since FY21
Gross margin fell when AN spiked, then rose with defence
EBITDA margin: ~20% for a decade, 28% now

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the FY24-26 margin step-up is real and mostly mix: defence (higher margin) went from a tenth to over a quarter of revenue, and the domestic explosives business, which is sold by tender, stayed flat. The swing factor in explosives is ammonium nitrate: Solar passes on most of a price rise with a lag, so revenue jumps and the percentage margin falls. That is happening again in FY27 (management: 18-20% of explosives growth is price).

bullets: **Broad-based beat.** All three lines grew 50%+; operating leverage on employee and other costs lifted the margin. Attributable profit was ₹653 cr (EPS ₹72.1).

**Against the FY27 targets.** Q1 revenue is 26% of the ₹14,000 cr target and defence 21% of the ₹4,500 cr target. Defence is usually back-ended (FY26: ₹418 cr in Q1, ₹1,008 cr in Q4), so the defence target needs ~₹1,190 cr a quarter for the rest of the year.

**No earnings call.** Solar filed only the fact sheet for Q1FY27; the 15-Sep Omnia call excluded questions on current operations. Order book ₹21,350 cr (defence ~₹18,000 cr); ~₹450 cr of the ₹2,050 cr capex spent in Q1 (ICICI Direct).

The less certain part is FY28-29: the defence order book has stopped growing and FY27 is inflated by input-price pass-through, which reverses if ammonium nitrate falls.

sections.title: Returns above 30%, but capex and working capital now eat most of the profit

blocks.p: Over FY15-26 Solar generated ₹7,290 cr of operating cash and spent ₹5,506 cr on capex, so free cash flow was only ₹1,784 cr against cumulative profit of ₹6,773 cr. Capex has stepped up sharply: ₹560 cr in FY24, ₹1,006 cr in FY25 and ₹1,739 cr in FY26 on Screener's cash flow (company: ₹1,182 cr and ₹1,556 cr for FY25-26), with ₹2,050 cr guided for FY27, for defence capacity (Nagpur, Dhule, Dholpur), new explosives plants and overseas units. Returns are still high: ROE was 32% and ROCE 38% in FY26, against our 12.5% cost of equity. Dividends are small (₹11 a share, ~6% of profit).

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** the business needs more capital than it used to. Defence plants, overseas units and working capital absorbed all of FY26's operating cash, and on our forecasts free cash flow is negative in FY27 (₹{{F.fcf.0|num}} cr) before turning positive. Then comes Omnia: ₹12,951 cr in cash, mostly borrowed. Solar's returns justify investing, but shareholders should expect debt, not cash, to build for the next two years.

sections.title: Earnings quality: profits are real, but cash lagged badly in FY26 and the definitions need care

bullets: **Cash lagged profit in FY26.** Operating cash flow was 36% of net profit in FY26 (₹621 cr vs ₹1,737 cr), after 192% in FY25 and 161% in FY24. Over FY15-26 operating cash (₹7,290 cr) slightly exceeded profit (₹6,773 cr). The FY26 gap is inventory (₹1,742 cr vs ₹1,040 cr) and receivables (₹1,858 cr vs ₹1,239 cr); management says the inventory build was deliberate.

**A recurring "below-the-line" loss.** Turkey is accounted for as a hyperinflationary economy; the restatement cost ₹94.5 cr in FY26 and ₹65 cr in FY25 (in other expenses). Other income of ₹128 cr includes a ₹68 cr foreign-exchange gain. Screener moves the Turkish loss out of operating profit, so its EBITDA margin (27.6%) is a little flattering; the company's own EBITDA (₹2,750 cr) includes other income.

**Minority interest.** ₹59 cr in FY26 (3.4% of profit) and ₹78 cr in FY25; EPS uses attributable profit (₹1,678 cr). Our model carries profit including minorities and divides by Screener's implied share count (9.4 cr), which keeps EPS on an attributable basis.

**Estimates in revenue.** The auditors' key audit matters are the "powder factor" provision (₹37 cr: a deduction from sales based on blast output achieved at customer sites, settled later) and the Level-3 fair value of ₹135 cr of unlisted equity and preference-share investments.
**Currency.** A weaker rupee lifted reported profit (export receivables) and added ₹276 cr of translation gains to equity in FY26; the reverse can happen.

**Disclosure gaps.** One reported segment, no EBITDA by line, no split of defence between India and exports, no Q1FY27 call. Investors are asked to trust a defence story they can only see in aggregate.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Audits are clean (S R B C & Co jointly with Gandhi Rathi & Co) and profits are cash-backed over time. The flag is for FY26's weak cash conversion, a recurring hyperinflation charge outside "EBITDA", and thin disclosure on the defence business that carries the valuation.

sections.title: From net cash to net debt in one year, as inventory and receivables ballooned

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 Solar had ₹1,524 cr of borrowings (incl. leases) and ₹767 cr of cash and investments: net debt of ₹757 cr, against net cash of ₹426 cr a year earlier (company: net debt ₹867 cr, 0.32x EBITDA). The swing came from working capital: inventory days rose from 95 to 130 and receivable days from 60 to 69. Management says the inventory was built on purpose "to mitigate the risk arising from geopolitical uncertainties" and should normalise "maybe in the next 2 quarters". Our model holds working capital at FY26's share of revenue, which is conservative if that happens.

sections.title: Ownership: the Nuwal family at 73%, Indian funds 12%, a thin free float

blocks.p: The Nuwal family owns 73.15% (Jun-2026), unchanged for years, with no shares pledged: Managing Director Manish Nuwal holds 38.93% directly, a family trust (Sohan Devi Nand Lal Nuwal Family Trust) 29.23% and Chairman Satyanarayan Nuwal 3.58% (Mar-2026). The trust received the 29.2% held by Kailashchandra Nuwal and his wife during FY26, after the Supreme Court disposed of his long-running case against the company. Mutual funds and AIFs own 12.46%, foreign investors 6.24% and the public 6.42%. Shareholders numbered ~117,000 at Jun-2026, double the Dec-2023 count.

sections.title: The street: 10 of 12 positive, targets bunched at ₹22,000-24,500, two Kotak sells far below

blocks.p: We found 12 notes standing on 30-Sep-2026: 10 Buy/Overweight and 2 Sell. Targets range from ₹10,300 to ₹28,160, median ₹23,162. Every broker that discloses a relative method uses **P/E**, at 50-70x on FY28E to Dec-28E earnings: Jefferies 70x Sep-28E (₹28,160), PL 62x Sep-28E (₹23,124), Antique 60x (₹24,418), Nuvama 55x Sep-28E (₹23,435), ICICI Direct 70x FY28E (₹23,200) and MOFSL 50x Dec-28E including Omnia (₹23,000; it cut the multiple because Omnia raises the non-defence share). The two sells (Kotak Institutional Equities ₹11,200, Kotak's private-client desk ₹10,300) use DCF. On Omnia the street is split: PL and Goldman Sachs keep it out of their base estimates, MOFSL includes it. Bulls focus on defence (Jefferies: defence from 27% to 40% of sales, 31% EPS CAGR); bears on valuation and the debt Omnia brings.

sections.title: Our honest summary: own the business on a pullback, not at 62x FY28E earnings

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's lowest-cost explosives maker with ~26% of the market, a fast-growing international business, and the most integrated private defence-energetics platform in India, with a ~₹18,000 cr defence order book, a 32.5% ROE and a founder-owner who has executed well for 30 years.

**What you are paying:** 73.8x our FY27E and 61.6x FY28E EPS, for ~27% EPS growth a year, with FY27 revenue lifted by input-price pass-through (18-20 points of explosives growth, per management). The price assumes defence (mostly exports we cannot see in detail) keeps compounding long after the current order book is delivered, and it ignores the debt and lower-margin earnings Omnia will bring. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a SELL.
